The 106,000 jobs that weren't, and the metal that took it straight.

The Bureau of Labor Statistics reported total non-farm employment down 23,000 for July against a consensus of roughly 83,000 jobs added, and revised June to a loss of 20,000. The unemployment rate edged down to 4.1%, which sounds like a contradiction until the participation rate is read alongside it: 61.4%, the lowest in more than five years. The rate fell because people left, not because they were hired.

Kitco's spot page closed Friday at 5:00pm New York with gold bid $4,341.30 an ounce, up $102.00 or 2.41% against Thursday. Silver closed $63.46, up 3.36%; platinum $1,743.00, up 1.46%; palladium $1,357.00, up 0.30%. Fine gold at that level is $139.58 a gram, against $138.72 on Friday morning. Outside sources do not agree on the exact mark: Trading Economics carried $4,343.43 for the same day, and Reuters reporting had spot near $4,356 at its intraday best. This paper carries the Kitco close because it is a stated closing print at a stated time.

What the print actually moved was the rate path. CME FedWatch had the probability of a September hike at 46% immediately after the release, down from 55% before it. Ellen Zentner of Morgan Stanley Wealth Management put the caveat where it belongs: next week's inflation data will likely be the deciding factor.

For anyone who buys metal by weight, the number that matters is $139.58 a gram. Ten grams of 18-carat gold, three quarters fine, now carries $1,046.85 of metal before a bench touches it. Across three sessions this week, gold has added 4.40%, and a manufacturer who quoted a customer on Wednesday and buys the metal on Monday is short that difference.

A signed 1960 costume bangle is carrying roughly five times the estimate of 2024 gold and diamonds — in the same sale.

Bonhams has put three Chanel sales on the September calendar across three cities. New York runs Chanel: From the Vault II from 7 to 17 September. Paris follows with a Vault II edition carrying roughly 400 lots, from 14 to 24 September. London closes the sequence with Designer Handbags and Fashion, 21 September to 1 October — and London is the one that concerns this desk, because it skews heaviest toward jewellery.

It carries a private collection of Chanel costume pieces from the 1960s through the 1990s, led by a filigree snake bangle made by Robert Goossens for Chanel Haute Couture around 1960, estimated at $13,000 to $20,000. In the same sale sits a pair of Chanel Fine Jewelry Comète Géode earrings from 2024, in 18-carat white gold and diamonds, estimated at £2,000 to £3,000 — about $2,690 to $4,040.

The rest of the series is priced as a volume business rather than a trophy one: New York leads with a gold-tone minaudière at $20,000 to $30,000, Paris with a tweed jacket at roughly $2,300 to $3,460. Four hundred lots at those levels is a sale built to clear inventory to a wide bidder base, not to set a record.

The signature is the material. A dealer reading these three catalogues twice will notice a house publicly stating that a documented Goossens for Chanel, in base metal and paste, is worth several times a current-production 18-carat and diamond earring from the same maison.

1,507 buyers gave two different answers, and the twenty-eight point gap between them is the story.

The Hong Kong Trade Development Council closed its twin jewellery fairs on 2 August and published what the floor told it. Asked which stone was most in demand, 29% said diamond, ahead of ruby at 25% and pearl at 20%. On a floor that has spent two years being told colour is taking the counter, the diamond still leads the demand question.

Asked a different question, the same floor gave a different answer. On growth potential, 57% named trendy fashion jewellery, 35% precious jewellery and 21% designer jewellery. The stone buyers are asked about and the product they expect to sell are not the same thing.

The metal answer sharpens it. Yellow gold was named the most popular precious metal by 40% of respondents, in a week that ended with gold closing at $4,341.30 an ounce. The metal the trade says it wants is the one that has repriced hardest against it — this paper filed China Gold Association figures Friday showing Chinese gold jewellery consumption down 33.88% by weight while bar and coin demand rose 28.42%.

On timing, respondents were cautious rather than pessimistic: one to two years before confidence is fully restored. A retailer reading only the 29% diamond figure will over-buy stones for a floor whose growth respondents put in fashion jewellery at 57%, and will discover the mismatch at the November reorder. Buy the diamond for the window and the fashion piece for the till.
